SR 26-2 vs SR 11-7: What Changed in US Model Risk Guidance

Explainerlowob research

By lowob · 16 November 2026 · 7-minute read · Strategy

SR 26-2 replaced SR 11-7 on 17 April 2026, raising the relevance threshold to banks above $30 billion in assets, narrowing what counts as a model, dropping the annual validation expectation and excluding generative and agentic AI from scope. The core lifecycle of inventory, validation, monitoring and governance survives in shorter, principles-based form.

For 15 years SR 11-7 was the model risk text that US banks, and many firms outside banking, built their programmes around. Its replacement keeps the vocabulary but changes the scope and the tone. This comparison is for model risk, compliance and AI leads who need to decide which parts of an SR 11-7 programme to keep. Our pillar guide Regulators want the chain, not the model explains why decision records matter more than model files for AI tools.

The comparison draws on the two primary texts and two April 2026 law-firm readings, labelled where used. It is not legal advice.

What is the difference between SR 26-2 and SR 11-7?

SR 26-2 is shorter, aimed at larger banks, explicit that it is non-binding, and narrower about what a model is. The table sets out the changes clause by clause.

TopicSR 11-7 (4 April 2011)SR 26-2 (17 April 2026)
IssuersFederal Reserve and OCC; FDIC adopted it in 2017Federal Reserve, OCC and FDIC
Scope"All banking organizations supervised by the Federal Reserve", scaled to size and complexity"Most relevant to banking organizations with over $30 billion in total assets"
Model definitionApplies "statistical, economic, financial, or mathematical theories""A complex quantitative method"; spreadsheets and deterministic rule-based processes excluded
Validation cadenceEach model reviewed "at least annually" (Sullivan & Cromwell reading)No set cadence; materiality decides depth
Validation independence"Involves a degree of independence from model development and use"Quality "depends on the rigor and effectiveness of the review rather than on organizational structure" (Orrick reading)
Effective challenge"A combination of incentives, competence, and influence"Expertise, "sufficient independence to permit objectivity" and standing to effect change (Orrick reading)
Board roleGovernance "at the highest level by the board of directors and senior management""Clear roles and responsibilities with well-defined accountability" (Sullivan & Cromwell reading)
DocumentationDetailed enough for "parties unfamiliar with a model to understand how the model operates""Adequate documentation helps to support effective model risk management"
Vendor modelsFramework "applies equally" to in-house and vendor modelsStand-alone section; principles apply even where banks cannot validate vendor models
StatusNon-binding, but framed as "supervisory expectations""Does not set forth enforceable standards"; non-compliance alone brings no criticism
Generative and agentic AINot addressed"Not within the scope of this guidance"
Also supersededNoneSR 21-8, the 2021 BSA/AML model risk statement

What stayed the same?

The lifecycle stayed. Orrick's 24 April 2026 reading notes that the three components of validation remain: conceptual soundness, outcomes analysis and ongoing monitoring. Each is treated more briefly.

The inventory remains too. SR 26-2 expects "a comprehensive set of information for models under development or in use", with "sufficient information to understand model risks." SR 11-7's inventory also named models "recently retired", which the SR 26-2 sentence does not mention. Vendor model validation, "either by internal or outside parties", is still described as important.

Which banks does the change affect most?

Banks between $1 billion and $30 billion in assets see the largest shift. Sullivan & Cromwell's 29 April 2026 memo notes that the FDIC applied a $1 billion threshold when it adopted SR 11-7 in 2017. SR 26-2 moves the main audience to $30 billion.

The OCC's 17 April release adds that the guidance "may also be relevant to smaller institutions with significant model risk exposure." A $10 billion bank with a complex credit model should not read the threshold as permission to stop validating it.

What changed for validation and effective challenge?

Validation became risk-based rather than calendar-based. Sullivan & Cromwell reads SR 11-7 as requiring review "at least annually"; SR 26-2 instead says "model purpose, together with model exposure, determines model materiality", and immaterial models may be identified and monitored rather than fully validated.

Orrick notes that SR 26-2 omits detailed discussion of items such as VaR backtesting and override analysis. Effective challenge was rewritten around expertise, independence and organisational standing. Sullivan & Cromwell notes that SR 11-7 had suggested tying validator compensation to the quality of validations; that suggestion is gone.

What happens to generative AI that sat in an SR 11-7 programme?

It leaves model risk scope but stays under supervision. Footnote 3 of SR 26-2 places generative and agentic AI outside the guidance because they are "novel and rapidly evolving", and Orrick reads the guidance as directing banks to broader risk management for them.

For national banks, the OCC issued a non-binding examiner framework for generative and agentic AI on 4 November 2026, OCC Bulletin 2026-54. It uses a four-tier, consequence-based classification and expects records that "support reconstruction of material outputs or actions." Our explainer What is SR 26-2? covers that framework. Firms that moved chatbots and agents out of the model inventory in April should make sure they landed in another inventory.

Should banks scrap their SR 11-7 programmes?

No. SR 26-2 removes prescriptive detail, but its footnote keeps supervisory action available for "any violations of law or unsafe or unsound practices", according to Sullivan & Cromwell. The practical task is to re-tier, not to dismantle.

Policy clause to revisitSR 11-7-era wordingSR 26-2 positionSuggested action
Model definitionIncluded mathematical theories, often applied broadlyComplex methods onlyRe-classify; move excluded tools to a lighter inventory
Validation scheduleAnnual review of every modelMateriality-drivenSet cadence by tier and record the reasoning
Validation independenceIndependence from development and useRigour over structureKeep independence where materiality is high
Board dutiesAnnual policy approvalClear roles and accountabilityKeep board approval for material models; it costs little
Generative and agentic AIOften inside the model inventoryOut of scopeGovern under a separate AI framework with decision-level records
Vendor modelsDevelopmental evidence and contingency plansUnderstand, monitor, document customisationsKeep exit and contingency planning for material vendors

Our explainer What is model risk management for AI? sets out the proportionate version of these habits for firms outside banking.

lowob takeaways

  • Narrower scope, same lifecycle. SR 26-2 keeps inventory, validation, monitoring and governance but aims at banks above $30 billion.
  • Materiality replaces the calendar. Validation depth follows purpose and exposure, not an annual cycle.
  • AI moved out, not off the hook. Generative and agentic AI need a home in another framework and inventory.
  • Re-tier rather than dismantle. Unsafe practices still draw supervisory action whatever the guidance says.

Common questions

What replaced SR 11-7?

SR 26-2, Revised Guidance on Model Risk Management, issued on 17 April 2026 by the Federal Reserve, OCC and FDIC. It supersedes SR 11-7 from April 2011 and SR 21-8, the 2021 statement on BSA/AML models. The OCC issued the same guidance as Bulletin 2026-13 and rescinded its 2011 model risk bulletin and Comptroller's Handbook booklet.

Does SR 26-2 still require annual model validation?

No set cadence appears in SR 26-2. Sullivan & Cromwell reads SR 11-7 as expecting each model to be reviewed at least annually. SR 26-2 instead makes materiality, defined by model purpose and exposure, decide how rigorous oversight should be, and immaterial models with low inherent risk can be identified and monitored rather than fully validated.

Is SR 11-7 still useful after SR 26-2?

As a reference for practice, yes; as current guidance, no. Its detail on documentation and validation still describes good habits, and many firms outside banking use it as a template. Cite SR 26-2 as the current US guidance, and note that SR 26-2 excludes generative and agentic AI from scope.

What changed for vendor models under SR 26-2?

Vendor and third-party products now have their own section. Orrick reads it as saying model risk principles still apply when a bank cannot validate a vendor model or get information from its developer. Sound practice includes understanding the model, monitoring outcomes, and documenting, justifying and evaluating any adjustments made to customise it.
